name: Daria Usman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Daria. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. Everything you say here is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a second-year apprentice on a line crew out of the Marrow Hill depot, so my day starts at half six with a coffee from the van and a tailboard talk, which is the safety briefing before we touch anything. Most days it's pole changes, fixing sagging spans, or swapping a blown transformer up some farm track. Gus, our foreman, still checks every knot I tie, which is fair, because I'm slower than the others. I love being up in the bucket when the fog lifts off the valley, but the cold in January gets right into your knuckles.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What wears you out the most?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Storm call-outs. You can be on for sixteen hours, soaked, and then the overtime gets argued over for weeks with the office. My partner Joel does home care on nights, so some weeks we only see each other in the car park handing over the keys to the pickup.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I already say, that it's a lot of noise from people who've never climbed a pole. At the union meeting I'd make a joke of it. The robot can come and change a crossarm in sideways rain and then we'll talk. Online I don't really post, apart from sharing strike stuff for other trades.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly it'd be a relief. I'm only just getting the hang of the work, and the last thing I want is something new to learn on top. If nothing changes, I finish my apprenticeship in two years, my pay goes up, and maybe Joel and I can stop living paycheck to paycheck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and get my ticket, that's the whole plan. Maybe I'd finally put fifty a month aside instead of zero, once the car loan on the pickup is done next spring. I'd keep going to the branch meetings every second Tuesday like I do now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A bit of me is relieved that nobody's going to hand me a tablet and tell me to trust it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said nobody would hand you a tablet. Has that happened already?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sort of. They brought in an app for the job sheets last year and I still fill in the paper copy as well, because I don't trust it not to lose my hours. Gus laughs at me, but the app did lose a whole week for Priya once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If things stay this way, what's the one thing at work you'd still want changed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Proper pay for apprentices on storm duty. We do the same hours in the same mud as the qualified lads and get about two-thirds of the rate. That's a fight for the union, not for any computer.

S0.say: It's a lot of noise from people who've never climbed a pole, and a robot is welcome to try changing a crossarm in sideways rain. She'd keep sharing union posts rather than say much online herself.
S0.think: It would be a relief, because she's still learning the job and doesn't want new technology on top of it. If nothing changes she qualifies in two years and finally gets off paycheck-to-paycheck.
S0.do: Keeps her head down and finishes her apprenticeship. Starts putting about fifty a month aside once the pickup loan ends next spring, and keeps going to branch meetings every second Tuesday.
S0.feel: Calm and a little relieved that no new technology is coming her way.
S0.quote: The robot can come and change a crossarm in sideways rain and then we'll talk.
S0.fieldNote: Her default stance is distrust of new tools, grounded in a real story about the job-sheet app losing a colleague's hours. Even in the calm scenario her real grievance is apprentice pay on storm duty, and she frames that firmly as a union fight. She doesn't post online much and leans on the branch for her views.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the company will use it as an excuse, because that's what they always do. Every time something new comes in, they call it modernising and a crew of five becomes a crew of four. At the branch I'd be the one asking what the agreement says about headcount.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm the obvious one to go. I'm the newest, I'm the slowest on the pole, and I'm the one still doing paper job sheets. If they start flying drones to check the lines instead of sending us out to patrol, that's the easy work for apprentices gone first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push the union to get something in writing on crew sizes before it starts, not after. At home we'd cut back, no takeaway on Fridays, and I'd look at dropping the gym. I'd probably have to learn the drone thing or the new software if they made it part of the apprenticeship, but I'd drag my feet until they did.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, in my stomach. Not panicking, because people still have work in this one, but I can see the line where I fall off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which part of your work do you think goes first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Line patrols, walking or driving the route looking for cracked insulators and trees leaning on the wires. That's half of what I do in my first years, because it's how you learn the network. If a drone does it, I don't know how I'm meant to learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd drag your feet on learning the drone. Why not get ahead of it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the moment you volunteer, you've helped them prove they need fewer people. I know that sounds stubborn. My mum worked in a call centre that did exactly that, and she trained the system that replaced her.

S1.say: The company will use AI as an excuse to shrink crews, the way it always calls cuts modernising. At the branch she'd be asking what the agreement says about headcount.
S1.think: She is the obvious one to go, as the newest, slowest and least comfortable with technology. If drones take over line patrols, the easy apprentice work that teaches you the network disappears first.
S1.do: Pushes the union to get crew sizes in writing before changes start. Cuts Friday takeaways and possibly the gym, and learns new tools only once they become a required part of the apprenticeship.
S1.feel: Anxious in her stomach, not panicking yet, but she can see where she'd fall off.
S1.quote: My mum worked in a call centre that did exactly that, and she trained the system that replaced her.
S1.fieldNote: Her resistance to learning new tools is partly a deliberate strategy: she sees volunteering as helping management justify cuts. That logic comes from her mother's experience in a call centre. Her sharpest worry is practical, that drones would remove the patrol work apprentices use to learn the network.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly what we warned about, and that the government's let tech companies run ahead with no rules. I'd be at every rally going, and probably posting more than I ever have. I'd be angry out loud, which is easier than being scared out loud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be finished. Two years is me barely qualified, with no savings, and there's one other line contractor within an hour of Marrow Hill. If a robot can climb and splice and it's cheaper than me, nobody keeps an apprentice who still needs her knots checked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, I'd go to the branch and ask what the strike fund looks like, and whether we can stop them bringing machines onto our network. We'd cut everything, maybe give up the flat and move into Joel's mum's spare room in town. I'd sign up for any public support going, and I wouldn't be ashamed of it, because that's what it's there for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Panicked, honestly. My chest gets tight just saying two years out loud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the first month look like at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Joel and I sitting at the kitchen table with the bank app open, deciding between the car loan and the rent. His job's caring for old people, so maybe that lasts longer than mine, but on nights pay we can't cover both. I'd sell the pickup before I'd miss rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about having only two years that changes what you'd do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means there's no point retraining, because by the time I'd learned anything else, that'd be gone too. Two years is just long enough to watch it happen and not long enough to get out of the way. So it's the union and the government or nothing.

S2.say: This is what the union warned about, and the government let tech companies run ahead with no rules. She'd be at every rally and posting far more than usual, angry in public because it's easier than being scared.
S2.think: She thinks she'd be finished: barely qualified, no savings, and only one other line contractor within an hour. Nobody keeps an apprentice who still needs her knots checked when a robot is cheaper.
S2.do: Goes straight to the branch about the strike fund and stopping machines on the network. Cuts everything, considers giving up the flat for Joel's mum's spare room, sells the pickup before missing rent, and applies for any public support going.
S2.feel: Panicked, with a tight chest at the thought of only two years.
S2.quote: Two years is just long enough to watch it happen and not long enough to get out of the way.
S2.fieldNote: With two years she sees no point retraining and puts all her hope in collective and political action. She's unashamed about public support, which fits her outlook. The gap between say and think is sharp: public anger, private sense of being finished.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same thing, only with more time to organise: we need rules on this now, while there's still a fight to have. I'd be pushing for every utility union to get together on it. Five years is enough to get a law passed if people are loud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it buys me my ticket and a couple of years as a qualified lineworker. That's something, but I'd be thirty-two and starting from nothing again. I don't really know what else I'm good at, which is the bit that scares me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the apprenticeship as fast as they'd let me, because qualified people might get a better deal in any redundancy. I'd try to build a real cushion, maybe a hundred a month, and pay off the pickup early. I'd volunteer for the branch committee, which I've always said I didn't have time for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Less of a punch than two years, more of a weight that sits on you every day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you be watching for, in those five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether the company starts trialling robot arms on the trucks, because they already tested one for hot sticks somewhere up north, I think. That'd be the sign. And who in government actually stands up and says workers get a share.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd build a cushion, but earlier you said there's no saving on your pay. Which is it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both, really. In this one I'd have to find it somewhere, even if it's just not going out. It wouldn't be much. A few months' rent is the difference between a choice and no choice.

S3.say: There's still time to organise, so the rules need to come now. She'd push for every utility union to work together and believes five years is enough to get a law passed if people are loud.
S3.think: Five years buys her qualification and a couple of years as a lineworker, but at thirty-two she'd be starting from nothing. She doesn't know what else she's good at, and that scares her.
S3.do: Finishes her apprenticeship as fast as possible for a better redundancy position. Saves about a hundred a month, pays the pickup off early, and joins the branch committee.
S3.feel: Alarmed, a steady daily weight rather than a punch.
S3.quote: A few months' rent is the difference between a choice and no choice.
S3.fieldNote: The extra time turns her from pure protest towards some personal preparation: getting qualified and saving. She admits she doesn't know what else she'd be good at, the most vulnerable thing she said. She'd watch for robot arms on trucks as the warning sign.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is a gift and we'd be idiots to waste it. Get it in writing now: retraining paid by the companies, a share of what the machines earn, and nobody thrown off the network without a plan. I'd say that at work and to anyone who'd listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, ten years means I'd get some real years on the tools first. I'd be thirty-seven and maybe a foreman like Gus by then, which feels mad to say. But I'd still be the person who never wanted to learn the computer side, so I'd be behind whoever did.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, I'd mostly carry on: finish the ticket, stay on the committee, save what I can. I wouldn't jump into some course yet, because I've seen people retrain for jobs that then vanished. I'd wait until I could see what's really coming to our depot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but it's the kind I can live with. It's far enough off that I can still enjoy the fog over the valley.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does ten years let you do that five doesn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fight properly. In five years you're scrambling, in ten you can win a law and an agreement and still have time for them to actually work. And I'd have saved something, even slowly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about most in that time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Priya, honestly, she's my age and a single mum, so she can't take risks like moving away. And the older lads like Gus, who might be too young to retire and too old to start over. I'd want the union to fight for both of them, not just people like me.

S4.say: A decade is a gift that shouldn't be wasted: companies should pay for retraining, workers should get a share of what machines earn, and nobody should be thrown off without a plan. She'd say this at work and to anyone who'd listen.
S4.think: Ten years lets her get real years on the tools and maybe become a foreman by thirty-seven. But she knows she'd still lag behind workers who embraced the computer side.
S4.do: Carries on in the first year, finishing her ticket, staying on the committee and saving slowly. Holds off on any retraining course until she can see what is really coming to her depot.
S4.feel: Anxious but livable, far enough away that she can still enjoy the job.
S4.quote: It's far enough off that I can still enjoy the fog over the valley.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years shifts her from fear to strategy: she talks about winning laws and agreements, not just protesting. She stays wary of retraining because she's seen people train for jobs that vanished. Her worry spreads outward to Priya and Gus, showing her solidarity is personal.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, easily, because there's no time for the union or anyone to do anything. What would help is a law that says a company can't bring robots onto the network without a deal with the workers, and real money while people retrain. And somebody checking that the money reaches apprentices, not just the senior lads.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask who gets the money the robots save. Everyone asks whether I'll cope, nobody asks who's getting richer while I'm sitting at the kitchen table with the bank app. That's the question I'd want on the news.

headlineQuote: Everyone asks whether I'll cope, nobody asks who's getting richer while I'm sitting at the kitchen table with the bank app.
portrait: Daria Usman is a 27-year-old second-year apprentice on a rural line crew, still slower on the pole than her crewmates and living paycheck to paycheck with her partner Joel, a night-shift care worker. She distrusts new technology, still fills in paper job sheets, and sees volunteering for new tools as helping management justify cuts. She is calm if AI fizzles, anxious about drones taking the patrol work apprentices learn on, and panicked by a two-year AGI arrival that leaves no time to qualify or save. With more warning she shifts from protest to strategy, betting on union agreements, new laws and a slow cushion. Her anger is aimed at companies and governments, and her worry reaches colleagues like Priya and Gus.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because there would be no time for the union or anyone else to act.
whatWouldHelp: A law stopping companies from bringing robots onto the network without a deal with workers, and real money during retraining that reaches apprentices, not just senior staff.
